parsed.narrative.subject: Dutch naval threat
parsed.narrative.summary: The narrator goes to White Hall to obtain a privy seal for felling the King's timber for the navy, then visits the Lords' House and the Exchange. At the Exchange he receives more bad news about a Dutch man-of-war capturing ships off the North Foreland near Margate. He notes this is a bold attack so close to England, and observes that the easterly wind both prevents English forces from Portsmouth from intervening and will help the Dutch escape. He prays for preservation and reflects on how the English have made the Dutch seem contemptible in their discourse. He dines with Mr. Hollyard, works late at the office until past 11, then goes home for supper and bed.

parsed.narrative.summary: The diarist attends a committee meeting at Mr. Povy's and Lord Ashly's, where Povy confounds himself with many words and no understanding, bringing disgrace upon himself and causing everyone to doubt whether he is a fool or knave. The business is referred to another meeting. The diarist notes with wonder that he sits with his hat on while Mr. Sherwin stands bare-headed as a clerk, but thanks God that he does not think himself any better for this social distinction. Afterward, he dines merrily with pheasants, laughing about Povy's folly, then works late at the office and visits Sir W. Batten where he notes he is "mighty great." He ends the day sorting books and noting the warming weather, hoping the frost will break.

parsed.narrative.subject: Samuel Pepys
parsed.narrative.summary: Pepys begins his day at his bookseller's, directing the rebinding of his old books to create a uniform study. He is summoned to dine with Lady Sandwich, who asks him to deliver a letter safely to Lord Sandwich at Portsmouth. During dinner, she raises concerns about Creed being suspected as a fanatic and false fellow; Pepys agrees Creed is shrewd and cunning, and Lady Sandwich concurs. Later, Pepys meets with Povy, Sherwin, Auditor Beale, and Creed to work on Povy's accounts, which Pepys finds extraordinarily complicated. After the others leave, Pepys persuades Povy to remove sums not yet realized from the account. He returns home at 9 p.m., vexed and with a headache, and goes to bed.

parsed.narrative.subject: Pepys's daily affairs
parsed.narrative.summary: Pepys begins his day at the bookseller's, arranging for his old books to be rebound to uniform binding. He is summoned to dine with Lady Sandwich, who asks him to deliver a letter safely to Lord Sandwich at Portsmouth. During their conversation, she raises suspicions about Creed being a fanatic and false fellow, to which Pepys responds that he considers Creed exceptionally shrewd and cunning, someone he would fear being outwitted by. Later, he meets with Povy, Sherwin, Auditor Beale, and Creed to work on Povy's accounts, which Pepys describes as the most confusing he has ever encountered. He manages to have sums not yet realized removed from the account before leaving at 9 p.m. He returns home vexed with a headache and goes to bed.

parsed.narrative.subject: Samuel Pepys
parsed.narrative.summary: Pepys spends a busy morning and dines at home on hare pie. In the afternoon he travels by coach to White Hall for Council but arrives too late. He returns with merchant Mr. Gifford and goes to a coffee-house where he meets Mr. Hill, who tells him he is to be Assistant to the Secretary of the Prize Office under Sir Ellis Layton at Sir Richard Ford's house. Pepys thinks this position is somewhat low but potentially considerable, and it changes his opinion of Hill's wealth and ability to provide for Mrs. Pickering. He then visits Sir J. Minnes, who is ill but improving, and hears about Sir Ellis Layton's past madness at Antwerp. He works late at his office, troubled by a cold and pain in his testicles from squeezing himself in a coach, then goes home out of order to supper and bed.

parsed.narrative.subject: daily rounds and office business
parsed.narrative.summary: Pepys rises and works through the morning, dines at home on hare pie, then goes by coach to White Hall for Council but arrives too late. Returning with merchant Mr. Gifford, they visit a coffee-house where Pepys meets Mr. Hill and learns of his new position as Assistant to the Secretary of the Prize Office under Sir Ellis Layton at Sir Richard Ford's house. This news causes Pepys to revise downward his estimate of Hill's wealth and prospects for Mrs. Pickering. He visits the still-ill Sir J. Minnes, hears gossip about Sir Ellis Layton's past madness, then works late at the office despite his cold and a self-inflicted injury from squeezing into a coach, returning home out of order for supper and bed.

parsed.narrative.summary: Samuel Pepys is visited by Jane Welsh, Mr. Jervas's maid, who has left her master to be with her sweetheart Harbing, a poor and worthless fellow. Pepys tries to dissuade her, takes her by boat to the Falcon where they talk for an hour or two, but she insists it is her fortune to have this man though she believes it will be her ruin. He then leaves her, changes, goes to the Exchange, dines with Mr. Povy and Creed, visits Lord Bellasses to discuss Tangier business, then White Hall where he delivers a letter to the Duke of York and has an extended conversation with Mr. Slingsby about the Mint, coinage, and trade policy, learning about money circulation and the folly of prohibiting bullion export. He ends by visiting sick Sir J. Minnes, seeing Mrs. Turner's rock, and working late at his office.

parsed.narrative.summary: Pepys begins the day with frustrating, uncertain work at Westminster regarding ships for Tangier, which he describes as servile. His wealth has decreased to £1257, and he stays up until nearly 2 a.m. working on his accounts.

parsed.narrative.subject: Samuel Pepys
parsed.narrative.summary: Pepys is vexed by uncertain business at Westminster regarding ships for Tangier, which he considers servile work. After dining at the Crowne tavern with colleagues, he returns home to find his wife demanding that he dismiss the maid Jane. Hearing both sides, he finds his wife at fault due to her excessive fondness for Tom, which displeases everyone else in the household. Following high words with his wife, he decides the maid must go but will also discipline the boy, whom he fears he has spoiled. To ease his mind, he settles accounts, making himself debtor for £117 5s. gained with joy the previous month but now likely to be refunded, concluding that a quiet mind and certainty of his own estate is worth all. He stays up until nearly 2 a.m. working on accounts.

Rider, Cutler, and Mr. Deering on hemp business, returns to White Hall for a failed meeting about navy debts, is taken to the Park by Lord Brunkard where he notes the dust and the presence of Mrs. Middleton as the only great beauty, and ends his day at his office where Mr. Warren proposes a financial arrangement for ship protection before he goes home to supper and bed.

parsed.narrative.subject: Tangier business trouble
parsed.narrative.summary: The narrator rises early to visit Mr. Povy regarding his Tangier business, desiring resolution to his troubled mind about whether Povy wishes to resume his position as Treasurer under terms offered by Lord Ashly. Povy refuses, initially satisfying the narrator, but Creed raises doubts about whether Povy must inevitably return due to auditors' reasoning. The narrator secures an order for Povy to pay remaining accounts to him. He dines with Creed, discusses Will Howe's dissembling, spends time at White Hall, walks with Wren and Ager, fetches his wife, goes to Mile-End Greene for cream and cakes, then returns home. He receives false news that the English and Dutch fleets are engaged and Captain Teddiman's legs were shot off, but later learns this is untrue—all are well, and the Royal Katherine has joined the fleet and proves seaworthy, which gladdens him for Christopher Pett and Captain Teddiman's sakes.

parsed.narrative.summary: The narrator visits Mr. Povy to resolve his anxiety about the Tangier business, offering to let Povy resume the Treasurership on his own terms. Povy refuses, initially satisfying the narrator, but Creed raises doubts about whether Povy must be reinstated due to auditor requirements. The narrator secures an order for Povy to pay remaining accounts to him. Later, false news arrives that the English and Dutch fleets have engaged in battle and Captain Teddiman's legs were shot off, causing alarm. By evening, corrected reports arrive: all is well, the Royal Katherine has joined the fleet and proves seaworthy, bringing relief.

parsed.narrative.summary: Pepys visits the Duke of Albemarle and reads letters about naval engagements: three Dutch privateers captured, including one commanded by Everson's son, but Captain Golding was killed in The Diamond. The Dutch fought stoutly against superior English forces. Everson, when captured, wished he had been killed rather than taken. News also came of the Dutch Smyrna fleet spotted near Scotland, prompting the King to order a northern fleet. The King then personally recognized and spoke with Pepys at White Hall about ships in the River, the first time Pepys knew the King knew him personally. Pepys dined with Creed, Sir W. Rider, and Cutler, then saw a play with his wife, missed finding Sir Ph. Warwicke, and worked late at his office. A silver watch was left at his house by Briggs, which angered Pepys because his wife accepted it and gave the messenger a tip, obligating them.

parsed.narrative.subject: Samuel Pepys
parsed.narrative.summary: Pepys walks with Sir Philip Warwicke in the park, discussing Sir G. Carteret's accounts with great delight. He then travels by water with his wife and Mr. Moore to Chelsea to obtain his Privy Seal for Tangier, but finds his Lord Privy Seal gone abroad and must return without landing. Later he succeeds in getting his commission for Tangier-Treasurer signed by the Lord Treasurer, along with the docquet for his Privy Seal regarding monies to be paid to him. He ends the day working late at his office before supper and bed.

parsed.narrative.subject: Tangier Privy Seale
parsed.narrative.summary: Pepys rises early and travels to White Hall and then Chelsea, where his fears about difficulties with his Tangier Privy Seale prove unfounded as Lord Privy Seal passes it readily and treats him civilly. He enjoys contemplating a beautiful portrait, then returns to London joyfully. After various social engagements including a dinner at Trinity-House and experiments at Gresham College involving Florentine poison on animals, Povy gives him discouraging news about money, plunging him into cruel melancholy. He consults with Creed about what to do, then returns home with a headache, to bed by 10 or 11 o'clock.

parsed.narrative.subject: Mr. Andrews's financial need
parsed.narrative.summary: Pepys spends the morning at the office, then dines with Mr. Povy, whose boldness with Mercer makes both her and Pepys blush. Afterward, Creed and Andrews arrive, and the main topic is Andrews's lack of money. Pepys resolves to lend Andrews 400 or 500 pounds secured by tallys, a decision that initially goes against his heart but is confirmed when Creed agrees to join him. He works late at the office, then learns that the first play has been performed in White Hall's noon-hall, now converted to a playhouse, though he could not attend despite his desire.

The evening ends with music, a technical argument about corants with Captain Taylor that vexes Taylor, and laughter shared with Creed afterward.

parsed.narrative.subject: pepys's sunday
parsed.narrative.summary: On the morning of April 22, Pepys threatens to dismiss his son's lute-master if the boy neglects his music, then works busily at the office. The next day, being Sunday, he takes his wife to White Hall Chapel in Mr. Povy's coach, leaves them in the Organ Loft, drinks at the Harp and Ball while chatting with a pretty maid, then hears young Stillingfleete preach a sermon on the King's Coronation day. Afterward they dine lavishly at Mr. Povy's, take the air beyond St. Pancras despite rain, and return home for music, supper, and a heated but friendly argument with Captain Taylor about the musical structure of a Corant.

parsed.narrative.summary: Pepys attends the office in the morning, then goes to the Exchange and has dinner with Creed. He wears his new expensive silk camelott suit to Sir Thomas Viner's burial at Goldsmiths' Hall. The crowd is so great that he and Creed step out to Pater Noster Row to choose silk for another suit. He returns home late, having forgotten his duties, with news that the English fleet has sighted Dutch ships.

parsed.narrative.subject: monthly accounts
parsed.narrative.summary: The subject spends the morning at the office and afternoon securing a warrant from Lord Treasurer, but is troubled by reports that Sir W. Batten and Sir J. Minnes notice his frequent absences from office business. He resolves to mind his business better and not neglect writing to Mr. Coventry, though he falls asleep while writing and blots the letter. On the 30th, he works alone on intricate monthly accounts, finding himself worth above £1400, the greatest sum ever, with over £100 gained this month. He dines with Mr. Spong, whom he admires for modesty and ingenuity, then visits Woolwich and Deptford. He ends the month content with his estate but troubled by expected difficulties over Tangier business, while noting great fears of sickness spreading in the City.

parsed.narrative.subject: Mr. Hater's release
parsed.narrative.summary: Pepys spends a morning at White Hall securing Mr. Hater's release on bail through Secretary Morris, with Mr. Hunt as co-surety. parsed.narrative.subject: Samuel Pepys
parsed.narrative.summary: Pepys wakes before 4 a.m. with painful urination, which he attributes to drinking too much cold drink before bed. He returns to sleep, then rises to work at the office where he is very busy all morning. At noon he dines with Sir G. Carteret and the Board, where they enjoy good food and discourse but fear fresh news of the fleet; they receive dubious news from Sir W. Batten at Harwich claiming the Dutch are beaten, which they all mock for its simple writing. In the afternoon he is greatly vexed at the office finding the Controller has done nothing to right the King's accounts. He writes letters, then coaches to Sir Ph. Warwicke's about Tangier money, and visits my Lady Sandwich, who awaits news of my Lord with remarkable calm temper. She tells him my Lord Rochester is out of hopes with Mrs. Mallett, and that the King may soon give leave for my Lord Hinchingbroke to pursue her. He returns home and to bed before midnight.

Pepys buys a coloured silk suit instead of his usual black, to celebrate the naval victory. He hosts a supper with guests including Mr. Honiwood and Roger Pepys, serving venison pasty in place of his postponed stone-feast, and enjoys the evening's merriment before walking with his guests to find a coach and returning home glad the event is over.

parsed.narrative.summary: Pepys rises with a headache from overthinking, then goes to White Hall and meets Mr. Moore, who reassures him about Lord Sandwich's reputation after hearing the King praised him. He notes the King's grief over Lord Falmouth's death, though others do not share it, acknowledging Falmouth's honor in dying with the Duke. Returning home, his servants prepare a supper to replace his cancelled stone-feast. He buys a coloured silk suit instead of black, celebrating the naval victory over the Dutch. He spends the day at the office, then at noon puts on his first all-lace band and dines at Kate Joyce's with his mother, wife, and many friends, receiving good treatment. He then purchases two more lace bands at the Old Exchange with his wife and Mercer, noting the prettiness of his seamstress with his wife's concurrence. He travels to Deptford and Woolwich to arrange housing for his wife with Mr. Sheldon, returns late, writes letters, and sups at home. He notes news favorable to Lord Sandwich and reports rising plague deaths in London.

parsed.narrative.subject: Duke of York's return from sea
parsed.narrative.summary: Pepys attends the office and learns the Duke of York has returned from sea and will receive them that afternoon. At White Hall, Pepys observes the Duke and his courtiers looking healthy from their time in the sun. He kisses the Duke's hands and waits all afternoon. Pepys is overjoyed to see Mr. Coventry, and they withdraw to the Matted Gallery to discuss business, including Lord Sandwich's honorable service, various captains' conduct, and naval appointments. Pepys notes the Duke tore up Captain Holmes's commission when Holmes rashly demanded promotion. He records casualty figures and Dutch claims of victory, then returns home to work late, finding his wife and mother still out.

Pepys notes the strange Dutch claims of victory despite a clear English triumph with minimal casualties. He works late and returns home to find his wife and mother still out.

The entry interweaves personal routine with the mounting catastrophe of the Great Plague.

parsed.narrative.summary: The writer spends the morning writing letters, including one to Lady Carteret about the city's health and sorrowful stories. After dinner, he goes to Greenwich to meet Sir J. Minnes and Lord Bruncker, waits for justices, then walks in the Park with companions, eating fruit from the King's garden. Lord Bruncker gives him a cane. On his walk home, he passes Coome farme where about twenty-one people have died of the plague, recalling a dead corpse in a coffin he saw unburied days before, and notes that a watch keeps people confined night and day, remarking that the plague makes people cruel to one another like dogs.

parsed.narrative.subject: Samuel Pepys
parsed.narrative.summary: The narrator walks with Captains to Greenwich, where they criticize Captain Teddiman's handling of the Bergen affair for delaying too long while the Dutch prepared. They sat late but accomplished little due to lack of money. He dined merrily with Lord Bruncker and his mistress, then examined Colonel Blunt's new spring chariot, testing it on rough terrain with mixed results. He drove himself to the office, finished letters, and spent a merry evening with W. Pen discussing travels and French manners before bed.

parsed.narrative.subject: Samuel Pepys
parsed.narrative.summary: Pepys wakes and discusses with his wife an anonymous letter; she convinces him she does not know its source, suggesting it may be from her cousin Franke Moore recently arrived from France. Deciding the matter is insignificant and unwilling to distress himself in a strange place during a melancholy time, he lets it pass and they are soon friends again. The day is spent on business, particularly investigating shipwrights who deserted work for three days due to lack of money, with hope they will return tomorrow. Lord Bruncker dines and stays through the afternoon. In the evening, a dispute arises over a book of Rates being transcribed by a Dutch clerk for Captain Millet's mistress; Pepys is reluctant but agrees to cancel the completed portions, which vexes the mistress who bears it with concealed malice. Pepys is troubled all day about his boy Tom who went to Greenwich and was delayed due to plague fears, but he returns safely that night.

parsed.narrative.subject: Samuel Pepys
parsed.narrative.summary: Pepys wakes and discusses with his wife a mysterious letter; she convinces him she does not know its origin, suggesting it may be from her cousin Franke Moore recently arrived from France. Pepys, being otherwise at ease and unwilling to distress himself in a strange place during a melancholy time, lets the matter pass and they are soon friends. The day is spent on business, particularly investigating shipwrights who deserted work for three days due to lack of money, with hope they will return tomorrow. Lord Bruncker dines and stays the afternoon. In the evening, a dispute arises over a book of Rates being transcribed by a Dutch clerk for Captain Millet's mistress; she is sent for, the finished portions are cancelled against Pepys's wishes, and she bears it with concealed malice. Pepys walks with his wife in the fields until night. Throughout the day he is troubled about his boy Tom who went to Greenwich and was delayed due to plague fears, but Tom returns safely having stayed at Mr. Hater's advice.

parsed.narrative.summary: The diarist records a day beginning with office business, then taking boat with Lord, Sir J. Minnes, Sir W. Doyly to Walthamstow where they enjoyed merry discourse about the previous night's revels, a plain venison dinner, billiards (winning an angel), and a prank pretending to have a warrant against Sir W. Hickes to vex him over his niggardliness. The prank was spoiled by feared betrayal from Sir W. Doyly. They returned homeward merry, then to Greenwich where the diarist received orders for Tangier payments, gave evasive answers about tallys, and ended at Woolwich playing tables with his wife before bed.

parsed.narrative.subject: Cocke's boy Jacke
parsed.narrative.summary: The narrator arrives at Greenwich with Lord Bruncker and Captain Cocke, only to learn that Cocke's boy Jacke has gone to bed sick, complaining of his head, which is considered a bad sign. Despite fear, the narrator stays and sleeps, then wakes to great joy at news the boy is well again. Later social events are disordered by Lady Batten's tardiness and a feud arising from Sir J. Minnes's perceived slight when guests apply to Boreman instead of him for supper, forcing the narrator to seek lodging elsewhere.

parsed.narrative.subject: Samuel Pepys
parsed.narrative.summary: Pepys records a day of business dealings aboard the Prince, including a £5,000 bargain for goods and his relief at avoiding signing for payment due to concerns about Captain Cocke's trustworthiness. After dining with Sir W. Pen and others, he and his companions took a wherry toward Chatham in the dark, suffering great difficulties when their waterman became lost. They eventually secured a fisher boy as guide who, despite his odd reticence, brought them safely to Rochester. During the journey they observed the sea-water glowing like fire at night, which sailors said foretold wind. They ended the night at the Crowne Inne, making merry with the boy who had not slept in a bed for seven years of his apprenticeship.

parsed.narrative.subject: Samuel Pepys
parsed.narrative.summary: Pepys describes a busy day at the office dealing with the burden of sick and recovered prisoners left on shore by captains who refuse to receive them back on board. He dines merrily with colleagues, reluctantly accepts gold from Mr. Deering, and gives alms to the poor wretches waiting outside. Upon returning home to his wife at Woolwich, he finds her distressed over a falling out with both maids, particularly Mary, who threatened to reveal something that would 'stop her mouth.' Suspecting it involves Brown and feeling jealous, Pepys initially storms out intending to return to ship, but decides to stay, reasoning that the Bezan won't leave until the next ebb, that trouble of mind is dangerous in this sickly plague time, and that servants cannot be dismissed now. He resolves to become pleasant with his wife and sleep contentedly, ending the month declaring it among the greatest three months of his life for joy, health, and profit, despite the plague season.

parsed.narrative.subject: Samuel Pepys
parsed.narrative.summary: Pepys spends a busy morning at the office dealing with the burden of sick and recovered prisoners who have no ships or money. He dines merrily with colleagues, reluctantly accepts gold from Mr. Deering whom he distrusts, and gives alms to the poor wretches outside. He then sails to Woolwich to find his wife distressed over a falling out with her maids, particularly Mary who threatened to reveal something. Though initially jealous and angry, Pepys resolves to suppress the matter, reconcile with his wife, and focus on his many reasons for contentment, ending the month with great satisfaction despite the plague season.

Coventry had long expected. After dinner he continues, but a long evening conversation with Gibson, who is departing for Yarmouth, reveals how little Pepys understands the victualling business and pursers' trade. This makes him ashamed and distrustful of his day's work, which he sets aside until morning. He then keeps his promise to return home for mirth, where neighbors Miss Tooker and Mrs. Daniels dance and stay merry until two or three in the morning, Pepys having gone to bed earlier.

parsed.narrative.subject: victualling business
parsed.narrative.summary: Pepys begins the day with resolution to work, hires Poynter as clerk, and spends the day alone in his closet drafting instructions for Surveyours of the Ports that Sir W. Coventry has long expected. After dinner he continues, but a long evening conversation with Gibson about to depart for Yarmouth reveals how little Pepys understands the victualling business and pursers' trade, causing him to distrust all his day's work and set it aside until morning. He then keeps his promise to return home for mirth, where neighbors Miss Tooker and Mrs. Daniels dance and remain merry below until two or three in the morning while he retires to bed.

parsed.narrative.subject: my last night's worke
parsed.narrative.summary: The writer discusses with his wife her permanent departure to London and arranges payments to Mr. Sheldon and Mrs. Barbary. He goes to the office where he has Mr. Poynter write out his previous night's work, which pleases him. However, he reflects on his lack of confidence in the work due to Gibson's earlier discourse, fearing he had done it poorly. Though Poynter and Mr. Hater approve, he suspects flattery due to his consciousness of his own ignorance. He dines with his wife, takes leave of her as she departs for London permanently, then returns to work at the office until past one in the morning.

parsed.narrative.subject: Samuel Pepys
parsed.narrative.summary: Pepys finishes his journal, arranges financial matters with Lord Bruncker and receives a bill of imprest from Captain Cocke. He visits Mr. and Mrs. Pierce, then goes to London where he and Pierce settle a bill concerning prize goods. At the Exchange, he hears troubling news that the plague has increased again despite recent frosts. He dines poorly with Sheriff Hooker but admires Hooker's son-in-law Lethulier and his wife. He then meets Captain Cocke and Sir W. Warren, arranging more financial dealings including potential insurance business. They seek the Duke of Albemarle's advice at the Cockpit but are rebuffed. He checks on his wife, learns with great trouble that his parish has the highest plague death toll in the city, and returns to Greenwich to conclude insurance plans with Lord Bruncker before going home to bed with his mind in great rest.

parsed.narrative.subject: Samuel Pepys
parsed.narrative.summary: Pepys walks to Redriff in frost, visits his wife and is briefly displeased by her attentions to her siblings, then clears his money matters to complete satisfaction. He spies Mrs. Daniel and Sarah in the street, follows them shyly but loses them. He dines merrily with Sir W. Warren, privately mocking Dr. Hinton's pretensions. After dinner he crosses the icy river home, frightened, then entertains Mrs. Tooker, Mrs. Daniel, and Sarah to cards and supper, enjoying great pleasure with Mrs. Tooker despite vexation that his name was used without permission in a shipping matter.

He spies Mrs. Daniel and Sarah, follows them shyly, loses them, and is invited by Sir W. Warren to dine at the Pope's Head where he inwardly mocks Dr. Hinton's pretensions. After business talk, he returns home by water, frightened by ice on the river. He entertains Mrs. Tooker, Mrs. Daniel, and Sarah to cards and supper, then learns from Mr. Pierce that W. Howe has used Pepys's name to secure passage for goods, and possibly Lord Bruncker's name too, which vexes him greatly though he conceals his discontent. The evening ends with card-playing and pleasure in Mrs. Tooker's company.
parsed.context.event: daily round of business and social calls

Batten discussing new instructions for signing and paying bills, and recommends Poynter for a clerk position to rid himself of someone unsuited. parsed.narrative.subject: Samuel Pepys
parsed.narrative.summary: Pepys rises early to meet with Lord Bruncker, Sir J. Minnes, and Sir W. Batten to discuss new instructions for signing and paying bills. He recommends Poynter as a clerk to the Controller to rid himself of someone unsuited to his own needs. At noon he dines merrily with Mr. Hill, Mr. Houbland, and their brothers at the Bear, then meets Mr. Andrews to arrange tallys for Tangier victualls, securing £210 profit for himself. He spends the evening watching Lord Bruncker disassemble and reassemble his watch, learning something new. He is vexed by a snappish answer from Madam Williams when he calls her a 'mad jade' in mirth, and by a letter from the Duke of Albemarle pressing continued Christmas meetings, which he had already intended. He makes up his journal for eight or nine days, easing his mind, and notes the continued frost with hope it will abate the plague.
